summary: ClassifyDesign's heuristic pass skips the RCT tier when the text credits a different study for the randomisation — within, nested in, participants in, recruited from, enrolled in, sub-study of, secondary analysis of, ancillary to — unless the title itself says randomised. The guard sits on the heuristic path only; an authoritative publication type still outranks it.
reason: A nested study names the trial it sat inside, and the heuristics cannot tell whose design they just read. One phrase in an abstract promoted a case-control study eight tiers to the apex of the pyramid, where it carried a high-confidence stance. Two wider rules were measured and rejected before this one: giving the title priority over title+abstract, and letting the title override the publication type. Both demote works whose titles legitimately name two designs — 'systematic review and meta-analyses' becomes systematic review — and between them they change seven works in the stored corpora, all in the wrong direction. The title exception is not decoration: a genuine RCT that reports a sub-analysis mentions its own randomisation the same way a nested study mentions its host's, and without the exception it would be demoted. The 60-character bound keeps the two halves of the phrase in one clause; unbounded, it joins an early 'within' to an unrelated randomisation sentence later in the abstract.
validated_outcome: Across the 249 works in testdata/corpora: 15 carry an RCT signal and none are flagged, 10 state RCT in their own title and none are affected, and no design or verdict changes on any corpus. Four tests, each verified by mutation: disabling the guard fails the nested case, forcing it always-on fails both the plain-RCT and the title-states-RCT cases, and removing the title exception fails the title case. A fourth test pins the limit rather than the fix — a publication type still wins, so a source that indexes a nested study under its host trial's type is unaffected.
